First, I brought in these small scotch eggs, which are pretty common in England. I usually share food with my friends because we often only have one person bringing lunch, so sharing is normal. My friend asked for some, and I gave her a few. Then another friend sat down and asked for one, and I agreed. So far, everything seems fine. Then comes M. She asked why, and I said because she didn't ask nicely. Then she apologized and asked again nicely, but I still didn't give her any because I thought she was just saying that because I told her to. In the end, I finished the eggs myself. Now, people are saying I'm the asshole for excluding her, but I was upset because she just lunged for my food without acknowledging me. Everyone else I shared with asked nicely. So, was I being unreasonable by refusing her after she apologized? Hmm, maybe I should consider why I was upset. It's not just about the food; it's about how she approached me. Lunging across the table without saying anything is pretty rude. It's like she didn't respect my space or my ownership of the food. So, in that moment, I felt disrespected, and that's why I pulled the eggs away. But then, when she apologized and asked again nicely, I still didn't give her any. Maybe I was holding onto my anger and not willing to let go, even though she tried to make amends. That could be seen as being stubborn or not willing to forgive. On the other hand, I was just trying to stand my ground because I felt like she didn't follow the basic courtesy of asking before taking. It's important to me that people respect my things, especially when it comes to personal belongings like food. I guess another angle is how the others reacted. Everyone else asked nicely, and I shared with them. So, why was M different? Maybe because she didn't follow the same protocol, and that's why I excluded her. But then, by excluding her even after she apologized, am I being fair? I also need to think about how this affects our friendship. If I'm too rigid about this, it might create tension between us. On the other hand, if I give in too easily, maybe I'm not setting boundaries that are important to me. Maybe I should have given her another chance after she apologized. It's possible that she was just having a bad day or wasn't thinking clearly. By refusing her again, I might have come off as unforgiving or too harsh. But then again, I was the one who was wronged in the first place. She disrespected me by lunging for my food without asking. So, shouldn't she be the one to make the first move in apologizing? But she did apologize, and I still didn't give her any eggs. I'm also considering the fact that I finished the eggs myself. Maybe that's part of the issue. If I had shared with her after she apologized, it would have shown that I'm willing to move past the incident. But by not sharing, I'm holding onto the grudge. In the end, I think I was right to be upset about how she approached me, but maybe I was too harsh in excluding her even after she apologized. It's a balance between standing up for myself and being forgiving and understanding. I guess I need to communicate with her about how her actions made me feel and why it's important to me that people ask before taking. That way, we can both understand each other's perspectives and work on our friendship moving forward.
